text: In the book's ε-δ definition of lim_{x→a} f(x) = L, the condition on x is written 0 < |x − a| < δ. What does the left-hand inequality 0 < |x − a| accomplish?
choices: It excludes x = a, so the limit depends only on the behavior of f near a, not on the value (if any) of f at a.
It guarantees that f is defined and continuous at a.
It forces the response δ to be smaller than the challenge ε.
It restricts attention to x on the right side of a only (a one-sided limit).
explanation: The book stresses that 0 < |x − a| explicitly excludes x = a, so the limit reflects only nearby behavior and f need not even be defined at a. Continuity, not the limit, is the condition involving f(a), and it drops the 0 < so that x = a is allowed. The δ and ε are chosen independently, and both x > a and x < a are considered, so the other options misread the definition.
